items.text: Thirty-two side stories for the Hook, drafted within canon from your waiting list (light ones mostly, a few dark). Do they stand as the list the jobs are built from when phase 3 comes? Read them under 'Read it here'; a note is optional.
items.recommendation: Yes: they keep canon and your rulings, and each ends in something the town remembers, which is what the game is about. Your note can strike or change any of them, or rule the three points named at the top. No web link: the stories are on this page.
detail: How they work: each is found on foot (overheard, asked in passing, seen through a window), never a marker; offered when something has happened, not at a set hour; the person waits a while, then stops waiting, and that is an ending too. Every ending changes what somebody in the street knows or says about Tom. Canon's rule throughout: adults only, no drink, no gambling, nothing sexual, no slur ever said, Tom never drives. None touches the fire, Mickey's real book, the sit-down, the inspection or the endings. Three points are yours inside them: the words on Mickey's sign (6); whether a story may lean on a main character's private life (4 Ron's Fridays, 18 Mickey's letters to June, 29 Ada's rent); and Mickey's mooring (17), a thing of his the draft invents. Checked against canon by one fresh reviewer, its twelve fixes made.

1. The long way round (grey; Act I; micro). Found: Sheila's fare book, once she lets him see the day book, or Pauline on the radio saying "Kevin's quiet again." Kevin Needham's day fares come in short against his mileage; he is running his own jobs in Mickey's car. Steps: the day book at the counter; Kevin's car on the rank, its mileage; Pauline's log; Kevin at the caff at his break. Ends: sack him (the rank is one car short; the drivers learn the new owner reads the book); let him keep it for a cut (a racket starts, and the fare book lies a little more); say nothing and pay the gap (Sheila sees it). If it goes wrong: Kevin hears he is being looked at and quits on the rank in front of the street. The town keeps: whether Tom reads the book.

2. Two real minutes (light; Act I; micro). Found: Pauline Kitching, mid-call, asks whoever is at the counter to take the phone for a minute. A caller wants a car "for the doctor's at ten" and will only give her name to Pauline. Tom can take the call, take the order wrong, or hand back. Ends: the booking is right and Pauline says "You'll do" to Terry that night; it goes wrong and the caller walks, telling the newsagent's queue Mickey's has gone to pot. The town keeps: Pauline's first word on him, which she repeats on the radio to both drivers.

3. The night lodger (light; Act I; micro). Found: Ian Megginson, passing the office door, says the front lock is "anybody with a hairpin and an hour", and the scratches on it are new. Norman Dent saw a light in the yard at three. Steps: the scratched lock; Norman on the warehouse row at night; the yard after midnight, where Darren Milner is asleep across the back seat of the spare car. Ends: throw him out (Darren tells the parade Tom is hard); let him stay as a night eye on the yard (Darren becomes Tom's, and talks about it); pay Ian for a new lock and say nothing. The town keeps: how the new owner treats a man with nowhere to go.

4. Mickey's Friday (light; Act I; micro). Found: Lily Tang, handing over Tom's first order: "Same as Mickey's? Every Friday, two of number nine. I remember." Steps: ask who ate the second; Ron, asked at the rank, goes quiet, then says "Fridays, aye." Ends: keep Fridays with Ron (Ron's loyalty takes a step; he tells Sheila); let it lapse; ask Lily to stop reminding him. The town keeps: Lily tells Peter, and Peter tells nobody, which is the point.

5. A coat from the back room (grey; Act I to II; micro). Found: Tracey Scarth, at her market stall or in the laundry's back room, sees Tom in his one jacket: "Mickey had a good coat. Bring it me, I'll take it in two inches." The coat hangs in the office. Steps: the coat on the office hook; Tracey's pins; June, if she sees it on him. Ends: wear Mickey's coat (Tom rises in clothes; the street reads him as Mickey's heir, and June goes cold); give it to June (she keeps it, or gives it back on her own terms); leave it on the hook. The town keeps: whose coat is walking down Quay Street.

6. The name on the board (light, with weight; Act I to II; micro). Found: Shaun Hewson, repainting the parade's boards this month, stops under Mickey's sign with his ladder: "Wants doing. What's it to say?" Ends: the old name fresh painted (the street reads continuity); the old name with "prop. T. Nowak" small underneath (the street reads a takeover, politely); leave it peeling (Shaun tells the caff the new man doesn't care). The town keeps: the sign itself, which everybody passes. For him: the sign's words are his to rule; the draft keeps Mickey's name in every ending.

7. A ride for the sergeant (grey; Act II; micro). Found: a rainy night, the phone rings and Pauline says, dry: "It's the police. She wants a car." DS Carol Ellis's own car has failed by the fish market. Steps: Terry takes the job; Tom can ride along, send Terry alone, or refuse the fare. Ends: the ride with her (a live talk in the back of a cab; she learns what he says and how he says it); Terry alone (Terry tells Tom what she asked him, or says "nothing" and means it); refused (Ellis walks home in the rain and remembers). The town keeps: Terry's version, told to Kevin.

8. Haddock's dear (light; Act I; micro). Found: Brenda Laverack, loud at her counter: her dawn order on the fish dock is coming up short and somebody is collecting it under her name. Steps: the fish market railing at dawn; the porter who signs for her boxes; the syndicate's man who takes the porters' cut. Ends: catch the porter yourself (a word, or fists, seen on the dock); pay Brenda's loss and say nothing; ask the Widow's people to sort it (it is sorted at once, and the dock now knows whose favour Tom asked). If it goes wrong: the porter sees him coming and the dock closes ranks; Brenda tells everyone he tried. The town keeps: Brenda's version, which the whole parade hears by noon.

9. Twelve weeks' notice (grey; Act I to II; micro). Found: Julie Kettlewell at the kiosk, fed up, telling anyone near that the steam laundry held back her last weeks' money. Steps: the laundry's office; its owner; Doreen Harland, who saw the pay packets made up. Ends: lean on the owner (he pays, and tells the harbour office clerk he was threatened); pay Julie from the office (Sheila marks it in the book); give her a job on the office phone beside Pauline. The town keeps: whether Mickey's still looks after its own, and who counts as its own now.

10. The laundry's hampers (light; Act II; micro). Found: Doreen Harland, at the laundry's side door with a stack of hampers and no van: "Your lot could carry these for us. Mickey would have." Ends: take the contract (clean money on the fare book, the drivers grumbling); turn it down; take it at a price too low to be clean, which Sheila will ask about. The town keeps: the cab office's name on the laundry's run, seen twice a day.

11. The window at the caff (grey; Act I to II; micro). Found: Grace Rinaldi's front window boarded one morning; she will not say who, and says "no police, and no fists either." Steps: Grace; Tracey, who saw a young man running; the newest of Danny Cammack's crew, a man of about twenty, on the corner. Ends: bring him to wash Grace's pots for a week, her justice (Grace forgets nobody); hand him to Ellis (Grace calls it police, which she said not to, and says so at the counter); hurt him (Grace bars Tom from the caff, and says why). The town keeps: that Tom did it Grace's way, or did not.

12. Closing time at the Tangs' (grey; Act II; micro). Found: at closing, young men in their twenties shouting at the takeaway's window; no words are heard, only the noise and Lily's face. Peter says it is nothing, as he always does. Steps: be at the counter at closing on the next nights; or Ron there; or speak to the men at the corner. Ends: presence alone ends it (Lily remembers); Tom humiliates the leader in front of the parade (it ends, and Danny's crew notices); nothing (it goes on, and the regulars see him not see it). Content: racism here is a fact about the men, never voiced and never rewarded. The town keeps: who stood at the counter.

13. Off the back of a lorry (light; Act I; micro). Found: Darren, on the pavement outside the office, with a crate of transistor radios (a made-up maker's name) and a grin: "Ten each to you. I owe you anyway." Ends: buy one (it works, for a week); refuse; make him pay off what he owes Mickey's first, in radios. If it goes wrong: the radios are the chandler's, and the chandler sees one in the office. The town keeps: what Tom buys and from whom.

14. Posters on the glass (light; Act I to II; micro). Found: every morning a fresh anti-poll-tax poster on Mickey's window (the town's own invented campaign, no real party or person). Its organiser, a woman from Fairview, asks if she may put one up properly. Ends: let her (half the street nods, the harbour office frowns); tear them down each morning (the campaign paints the kerb instead); let both sides post. The town keeps: which side of the window the office is on.

15. Half the berths empty (dark; Act II; micro). Found: Colin Mastin, at the crane's foot at the end of a shift, asks Tom straight: the Widow's people have offered dockers night work off the books; should he take it? Steps: Colin; the night berth; one night's look from the fish market railing. Ends: tell him to take it (Tom has a man inside the syndicate's nights, and Colin's risk is on Tom); tell him not to (Colin is short, and resents it, or thanks him); give him driving work on the rank. If it goes wrong: Colin is caught on the berth one night, and the dock decides whose man he was. The town keeps: who Colin says he asked.

16. The name board (light; Act I to II; micro). Found: Albert Suggitt, mending nets, mentions his old boat's name board went for scrap. It is at Dennis Iveson's yard on the warehouse row. (The boat's name is minted for the game; this one is a placeholder.) Ends: buy it back at Dennis's price (Dennis remembers who pays fair); take it (Dennis remembers that too); tell Albert it is gone. The town keeps: Albert's story of the board, told at the caff for weeks.

17. Mickey's mooring (grey; Act II; micro). Found: Gary Mawer at the caff, over a bacon sandwich: Mickey rented a mooring at the yard, three months unpaid, and nobody's boat is on it. Steps: the yard; the bill; the Widow's man, who asks about the mooring the same week. Ends: pay and keep it empty (the Widow notices a man keeping a berth he does not use; boats stay scenery); let her people have it (money, and a debt of goodwill she will call in); let the yard take it back for the bill. The town keeps: whether the new owner is in the boat trade, which is the dock's real question.

18. The ferry parcel (grey; Act I to II; micro). Found: Gordon Leckenby, at the landing: a parcel in Mickey's hand, addressed to June at an old address across the water, came back on the boat marked "not known", and was left at the landing for Mickey's. Inside, letters to her, years of them. Ends: give them to June unopened (her thread moves; she may speak to him at last); read them first (Tom learns something of Mickey, and June can tell); burn them. The town keeps: how June is with Tom afterwards, which the street reads at once; Gordon only talks about the weather.

19. The quiet quay (grey; Act II to III; micro). Found: Susan Coverdale, the customs officer who lives past Rita's, asks for a car at night after a late turn, and talks in the back. She notices things for a living. Steps: her late fares, two or three nights, Tom along or not. Ends: straight rides and straight talk (one careful officer who thinks him honest, and says so to people she trusts); use her talk for the night business (she notices that too); refuse her fares. The town keeps: what one careful woman tells her colleagues.

20. All on the forms (grey; Act II; micro). Found: Christine Pickering, harbour office clerk, at the newsagent's: a stranger has been asking at the harbour office who holds the lease on the yard behind Mickey's. She thought he ought to know. Ends: thank her (a source in the harbour office, who expects only manners); press money on her (she is insulted, and stops telling him things); ignore it (he never learns who asked). The town keeps: a clerk's opinion of his manners.

21. Lilies (light; Act I; micro). Found: Winifred Duggleby, doing the chapel's flowers: "Nobody gives lilies any more." It is her husband's anniversary on Sunday. Steps: the market in Copper Row, by a car from the rank. Ends: lilies on the altar (Winifred tells the whole chapel; Father Walsh hears who sent them); chrysanthemums again. The town keeps: a kindness, told after the service.

22. Father Walsh's rounds (light; Act I to II; micro). Found: Nora Cronin, at the grocer's: the priest walks to his sick calls at night in all weathers and will not take a lift as charity. Could a car "just happen" to be passing? Ends: arrange it quietly (Father Walsh guesses within a week and says nothing, which is his thanks); tell him outright (he refuses, kindly); leave it. The town keeps: Nora's protectiveness turned his way, or not.

23. Lead off the roof (grey; Act II; micro). Found: rain through the chapel roof onto Winifred's flowers; Dennis Iveson has bought a stack of lead "fair's fair" from two of Danny Cammack's men. Steps: the wet altar; Dennis's scales; the two at the corner. Ends: buy the lead back for the roof (Dennis profits twice and knows it); lean on the two (they return the money, and Danny hears Tom touched his crew); give Ellis their names (whoever saw him at her car says so; the parish does not thank a grass, and Danny's crew asks who it was). The town keeps: who mended the chapel, which the parish says from the pulpit as a thank-you, no name or a name.

24. Sign there, dear (light; Act I to II; micro). Found: Edith Stockill at the pension counter has the newsagent as one witness to her will and asks Tom, a stranger, to be the second, because "everybody else round here talks." She leaves her savings to the parish. Ends: witness it and keep it (it never reaches the street, which the simulation proves; Edith tells Sheila he can be trusted); witness it and let it slip (Edith hears it back within a week); decline. The town keeps: Edith's word to Sheila, or the street's knowing what it should not; either way, how he keeps a confidence.

25. Looking costs nothing (grey; Act I; micro). Found: Rita Welburn, polite at the pawn's counter: Mickey's watch came in the week he died. She will not say who brought it until Tom redeems the ticket. Steps: the ticket; Rita; Hal, who knows already. It was Ron, for the funeral flowers. Ends: redeem it and give it back to Ron without a word (Ron's loyalty takes a big step); ask him why (he tells, and is ashamed); leave it in Rita's window, where the street can see Mickey's watch for sale. The town keeps: Hal hears on Monday whatever happened.

26. Monday at Hal's (light; any act; micro, repeating). Found: Hal Metcalfe, in the coin shop that sells no coins: "It's the company I keep the shop for." Come by on a Monday with the paper and he will talk. Ends: Monday visits (each week Hal tells Tom what the street is saying about him, a day before he would hear it, through the gossip the simulation already keeps); none. The town keeps: that Tom sits with Hal; and Hal remembers everyone's business, Tom's included.

27. Friday means Friday (grey; Act I to II; micro). Found: Sylvia Rennison, on her step in her slippers: a lodger is three weeks behind and he is one of Danny Cammack's. Mickey would have had a word. Ends: send Ron (it is paid; Danny's crew hears Mickey's is still Mickey's); pay it yourself (Sylvia is grateful and tells nobody, then everybody); refuse, "I'm not Mickey" (Sylvia repeats it, word for word). The town keeps: the phrase Tom used.

28. One way (light; Act I to II; micro). Found: Karen Grummitt at the ferry's ticket window, quietly: a car at five on Thursday, with her case, and not a word to Mrs Rennison, whom she owes a fortnight. Ends: the car at five (she gets away; Sylvia learns whose car and is cool with Tom for a month); tell Sylvia (Karen stays, and hates the Hook a little more, and him); pay her fortnight for her and send the car. The town keeps: Sylvia's version, or Karen's postcard to the ticket window.

29. The rent on Ada's window (grey; Act I; micro). Found: Dawn Pybus, apologetic, with her clipboard on Ada's step: the landlord has raised Ada's rent, and Ada has said nothing. Sheila, asked, admits Mickey paid the difference without Ada knowing. The landlord's agent is a firm in the Exchange. Ends: keep paying it in secret (Ada never knows; Sheila does, and it counts); tell Ada (she refuses his money and her tea goes cold, or she takes it and is ashamed); let it stop (Ada moves her chair from the window to the back room, and the street notices its watcher gone). The town keeps: who keeps Ada at her window. Beside: the outline's "Ada's tea is the week's first test"; this story is offered only after that test, never before.

30. The lamp outside Ada's (light; Act I to II; micro). Found: Ada, at her window: the lamp outside has been out for weeks, the council will not come. Steps: the kiosk and the council's number; the harbour office; the harbour office's works man, who can get a lamp seen to for a favour. Ends: fixed through him (a small favour owed); fixed by Ian with a ladder, against the rules (a lit pavement, and a council letter); left dark. The town keeps: the light itself, every night.

31. Nothing moves but me (dark; Act II; micro). Found: Norman Dent, glad of company on his round, mentions lights in an empty warehouse: crates of car radios, Danny's crew's. He wants nothing but a flask of tea and someone to tell. Steps: the row at night; the warehouse; the crates. Ends: tip Ellis (the crew loses its stock, and Norman becomes a witness who saw Tom ask; who else saw is the simulation's); take the crates and sell them through the back of Rita's (money, and Danny's grudge); warn Danny (a favour owed). The cost Tom can see: Norman misses nothing on that row, Tom's own nights included. The town keeps: whatever Norman saw, which is everything.

32. The camcorder (dark; any act; micro; offered only if Tom did something seen and filmed). Found: canon's one camcorder in town has Tom on a tape: whatever he did on the street that its owner filmed from a window (the simulation decides whether anything was). Its owner is minted when the camcorder is placed; the draft gives it to Hal. Ends: buy the tape (it is gone, and Hal knows its price); take it (Hal tells everyone a tape existed, which is worse); let it lie (it reaches Ellis or Alison, by the gossip's own routes). The town keeps: a picture, the one witness that does not forget.

The texts follow: three backstories and 32 side-story outlines, in the model's words, reviewed once (34 passed, Sheila's after cutting three lines that broke the content rule). Every [invented] mark waits for you; nothing here is canon or built.
RON KIRBY (BACKSTORY)

Ron Kirby came to the quay at eighteen, in 1950, on his father's word to a gang foreman at a gate in the old port. He had been a labourer before that, nothing worth the telling; the quay was where he became what he is [invented]. He was taken on as a casual and was registered within the year [invented]. He worked the general cargo berths for thirty years, hooks and slings and then, as the cranes took over the lifting, the long walk behind a load, guiding it down. He was never a foreman and never wanted it. He was a man other men liked to have in their gang, because he was big, slow to anger and did not talk out of turn [invented]. His nose was broken in a hold in the sixties; the blue on the backs of his hands is older than that [invented].

He lives in two rooms on Tannery Row, in Ironside [invented]. There is no phone, so he uses the box on the corner, and the evening paper goes folded in his coat pocket. He was married once; his wife went to her sister's up the coast in the seventies and the marriage ended by degrees rather than by any row [invented]. He does not speak of her and no one asks. There is no one in his life now who depends on him, and the money he is short of goes on his rent, the odd round of tea and bacon rolls for other men, and the habit of being the one who has a tenner when someone needs one [invented].

He came to Mickey's by way of the street rather than the job. Mickey Suddaby drank his tea at the cafe across from the parade and Ron ate his breakfast there, and over some years the two men got to nodding, then to talking [invented]. When the dock labour scheme ended in July 1989 and more than half the registered dockers' jobs went, Ron's went with them. He was fifty-seven. The letter that came was the kind that did not need reading twice. Mickey heard within the week and put him on the door and the rank at the office, for a wage that was light even then and that Ron never once raised [invented]. He has said, and means it, that he does not forget it.

What Mickey was to him was a man who paid on the day and asked nothing about the rest. Ron did not know the whole of Mickey's business and did not ask to. He knew the door, the rank, the yard gate and who came and went at night; the rest was Mickey's and Sheila's. He was grateful in the plain way of a man who has been let go by an institution and picked up by an individual. It was Ron who found him, early one morning at the office, when he came on at the rank. The doctor said it was his heart. Ron has told it the same way each time it has been asked, and it has not been asked often.

On Quay Street he is close to a few people and easy with many. Sheila Dunn he has known since she started at the office, and the two of them keep the place going between them without ever having said so [invented]. Darren Milner owes him small sums and pays them back eventually. Ada's window gives onto his rank, and each knows the other is looking [invented]. The sign painter, the net mender, the crane driver and the lad on the quay he nods to as men he has worked beside, which in several cases he has. Father Walsh calls on the old, and Ron, who does not go to mass, does not turn him away at the gate.

His days run to a pattern. He eats at the cafe at seven, takes the rank from eight, and goes down to the fish front at noon and is back on the rank by one. In the evening he walks to the quay for an hour, because he cannot yet stay away from it, and is back at the office from seven until eleven to watch the street. Sundays he spends at the allotments, where he has a plot he grows onions and potatoes on [invented]. Fridays he ate from the Tangs' takeaway with Mickey; he says nothing about that and nobody pushes him to.

Three weeks on, with Mickey gone and a nephew from nowhere in the flat upstairs, Ron stays on the door out of habit and has not been told to stop. He wants to be told where he stands before he has to ask. He does not know what the new owner is or what he will keep, and he will not say so. He watches the stranger the way he watches the weather, for what it is about to do to his evening. He fears the letter, a second one, the kind that ends a thing without an argument. He keeps one private matter: that the week Mickey died he took something of Mickey's to Rita's and put the money into the funeral flowers, and told no one [invented]. He would sooner be thought short than be thought sentimental.

INVENTIONS:
- Taken on as a casual, registered within the year
- Well liked in his gang; quiet, slow to anger
- Nose broken in a hold in the sixties; tattoos older
- Lives in two rooms on Tannery Row, Ironside
- Married once; his wife left for her sister's up the coast in the seventies
- Spends his money on rent, rounds of tea and rolls, lending tenners
- Mickey's wage to him was light and he never raised it
- Ada and Ron watch each other across the rank
- He does not go to mass
- Onions and potatoes on his allotment plot
- He keeps the pawn private; that he told no one is stated, not his motive beyond pride

SHEILA DUNN (BACKSTORY)

Sheila Dunn was born in 1937 in a terraced street on the far side of the river, in a house her mother kept so clean that visitors took their shoes off without being asked. [invented] At eighteen she was a typist in the office of a coal merchant's on the Ironside side of town, learning shorthand at night classes and finding she liked figures better than letters. [invented] She married at twenty, a lorry driver named Harry Dunn, and lost him at forty-four to a lorry's brakes on a wet hill road outside the town. [invented] She has not remarried and does not discuss it.

She came to Mickey's in 1959, at twenty-two, when it was not yet a minicab office but a small car-hire firm: three saloons, a telephone and a man who needed his sums done. [invented] The cars went over to fares as the trade changed, and Sheila went with them. Nobody asked her to learn the new books; she learned them. Over thirty-one years she has kept two sets of them: the day book and the fare book, which the world may see, and the other one, which it may not. She knows exactly which pages are true. She does not say so, and it is the reason she is still there.

Mickey Suddaby, as she knew him, was a man who paid on the day and never raised his voice, which she found more frightening than shouting and more restful. He was careful with cash and careless with himself. He ate standing up and let the stairs between the flat and the office do his exercise. He asked her opinion of people before he took them on, and mostly took the other view, and was wrong about as often as he was right. [invented] He quietly paid the difference when a landlord raised Ada's rent, and Sheila knew, because it went through the book. She will admit it if asked and not otherwise. When he began to look tired, she noticed and said nothing, and has thought about that silence a good deal since. Near the end he asked her to promise something about whoever came after him, and she did. She keeps promises as she keeps figures.

Her friends on Quay Street are few and old. Ron Kirby has kept the door and the rank since the docks let him go, and she has known him long enough not to need him to talk. Ada watches the street from her window and is the nearest thing Sheila has to a confidante, though they would both deny the word. Edith Stockill at the newsagent's pension counter trusts Sheila's reading of people, which Sheila considers a misplaced compliment. Darren Milner she tolerates the way one tolerates weather.

The end of the dock labour scheme in July 1989 did not touch her wages but touched everything round them. More than half the registered dockers' jobs went, and the fares that had kept the office steady, men going off shift, men going to the hiring hall, thinned out by autumn. Mickey's has made little money since. She watched the takings fall in her own handwriting. Ron lost his place on the docks and gained a door to mind; she was glad of that and never said so.

Her days run on a short track. On weekdays she is at the office from nine, goes to the fish front at noon for what she calls her air, is back at one, and sits on the step at Rita's from five until six, watching the street go by before she goes home. Thursday begins at the pension counter, collecting what the state owes her, and she is at her desk by ten. On Saturday she works the morning and is finished by one. Sunday she does not work, and no one in the Hook has seen where she goes. [invented] The office opens at seven and she does not keep those hours; that is for the drivers and the dispatcher.

She dresses the same way each day, hair set weekly, cardigan buttoned, spectacles on their chain. She smokes, steadily and without ceremony. She keeps the key to Mickey's own room, which has been locked since he died, and she does not open it.

Three weeks ago, early in the morning, Ron found Mickey at the office and sent for the doctor, who said it was his heart. Sheila came in to find it done. Two nights before that she had seen Ron arguing in the yard with a stranger, and she saw what she saw and nothing more. She has told no one, and has not decided whether she will.

What she wants now is plain and she would never put it so: for the office to go on, and for herself not to be put out with it. She is fifty-three, with a council flat and a pension some way off, and she has spent thirty-one years being the one person in the building who is never surprised. The stranger who owns it now arrived with a suitcase and a letter, and she showed him round and stopped at the one door she does not open. She has not yet decided what to call him. She will decide when she knows. She fears, quietly, that she will like him, and that liking will not be the same as being able to trust him, and that Mickey's own judgement of people was never as good as he thought.

INVENTIONS:
- Born 1937 in a terraced street across the river; house kept spotless
- Typist at a coal merchant's in Ironside at eighteen; night-class shorthand
- Married Harry Dunn, a lorry driver, at twenty; widowed at forty-four by a lorry brake failure
- Mickey's in 1959 was a small car-hire firm with three saloons, later turned minicab
- Mickey paid on the day, never raised his voice, ate standing up, took the opposite view of her opinions about hiring
- Mickey asked her to size up his heir near the end (the promise itself is canon; the circumstances of its asking are not)
- Ada is the nearest thing Sheila has to a confidante
- Sunday: nobody knows where she goes

DARREN MILNER (BACKSTORY)

Darren Milner turned eighteen in 1983, the year the training scheme took him. He was placed at a joiner's yard on the edge of a northern town, described only as that: a town two hours from the coast by bus [invented]. He swept up, fetched tea, and was let go with the rest of his intake when the year ran out, a card in his pocket and nothing to show for it. He tried the scheme once more, at a warehouse, with the same result. After that he stopped looking for jobs and started looking for who knew about them. That was the trade, and it never changed.

He came to Meridian in 1986, in a mate's van, to help shift a load of something that fell through, and stayed because there was somewhere to sleep and everyone talked [invented]. The somewhere was his mother's. She moved to Meridian the year before, into two rooms off Weighhouse Lane in Copper Row, and Darren has had the box room ever since [invented]. Some nights he sleeps across the back seat of Mickey's spare car in the yard instead: when he has been out too late, or his mother has locked up on him, or he owes her more than he can stand to hear about, he goes to the yard. Mickey knew and said nothing, and left the yard gate on the latch [invented].

He came to Mickey's by being useful. The first thing he did was pass a message: a driver wanted by his wife, a call left with the dispatcher, Darren running it the length of Quay Street for nothing. Mickey noticed the nothing. He never gave Darren a job, because Darren is not a man you give a job to, but he gave him tea, a cigarette, the odd tenner, and the use of the rank as somewhere to stand. Darren heard Mickey speak of his nephew now and then, a name and not much more, and never thought it would come to anything. He had never met the man before the suitcase arrived. Mickey was the first person in the Hook who treated him as worth the bother, and Darren has not said so to anyone, which for him is a kind of grief.

The dock labour scheme ending in July 1989 did not touch him directly, since he was never on the books. It touched everything he sells. Men with redundancy money and nothing to do have time to talk, and men who used to carry the news from the quay to the caff now stand on the pavement instead. Information got cheap and then got scarce, because people grew careful. Darren learned to price it by the day. He owes Mickey's money already, a few hundred over the past year in small advances that were never written down except in Sheila's book [invented]. He knows she has it all. He is friendly with her in the way a man is friendly with his own debt.

His day runs to a clock he keeps without a watch. Mornings are the cafe, where he drinks tea slowly and listens to who comes in. Then a step or a wall near Rita's, the docks on Tuesdays and Thursdays, the market on Fridays and Saturdays; the fish front and the laundry front at midday, because the women there talk and the men there think they don't. Three in the afternoon, always, he is on the rank at Mickey's, and he is back there at seven. In between is the quay at five. Weekday evenings he works the warehouse row, where the watchman will trade a story for a cigarette, or the cafe on Tuesdays and Thursdays. By ten he is off the street. Sundays are the kiosk at one and the rank by three, and nothing else; Sunday is the day he thinks.

The pager is the thing he cannot afford. It is rented, a month behind, and he wears it on his belt where it can be seen [invented]. It rarely goes off. When it does he steps away to the nearest phone box with the look of a man in demand. Mostly it is his mother, or a cousin of someone who works at the depot, or a favour being called in. He leaves his messages with the dispatcher at Mickey's, and takes other people's the same way, so his whole life runs through that radio and that phone. That is why Mickey's matters to him more than he would admit.

What he wants now is to stay on the right side of whoever owns the rank. He has watched the stranger since he came, the way he watches everything: who talks to him, who stops when he comes near, what Ron's face does when the new owner gives an order. He has not decided what the man is worth. He is afraid of being caught holding something that belongs to someone else, afraid of Ron, afraid of the men he has told too much, and afraid, quietly, that the new owner will tidy the office and tidy him out with it. He would sell nearly anything, except that he will not make up what he has not heard. A liar gets found out on the street, and then nobody tells him anything.

INVENTIONS:
- Darren's home town: a northern town two hours from the coast by bus, unnamed.
- Joiner's yard placement on the first scheme, swept up and let go.
- Second scheme placement at a warehouse.
- Came to Meridian in 1986 in a mate's van, to shift a load that fell through.
- His mother moved to two rooms off Weighhouse Lane in 1985; he has her box room.
- Mickey left the yard gate on the latch and knew Darren slept there.
- A few hundred pounds owed to Mickey's in small unwritten advances, recorded in Sheila's book.
- The pager is rented, a month behind, worn where it can be seen.

- His voice is a young northern Englishman's but his home town may not be named; it is left as an unnamed northern town and it must stay unnamed.
- The routine puts him at the quay at 17:00 and the warehouse row at 20:00; no reason is given beyond his trade, as the sources give no reason.
- The casting sample line's real town (a lift to Grimsby) was not used, so that line needs a rewrite elsewhere.
- Story 13 (crate of radios of a made-up maker) was not touched here, to avoid pre-empting that story's turn; only the debt it assumes is established.
- The Wednesday and Friday routine differences (kiosk, market, Rita's step) are given only as places; no reasons invented beyond his trade.

Fixed:
- "the pub" became "the caff" (canon allows pubs only as buildings, never as where men meet).
- Weighhouse Lane is in Copper Row, not the Hook: his mother's rooms now say Copper Row.
- Two sentences quoting his casting sheet and "the side stories" inside the prose were cut to one plain sentence.
- "watched the stranger for three weeks" became "since he came": Tom arrived three weeks after Mickey died, not three weeks ago.
- GAPS put in the third person.
Not fixed: Where Darren sleeps is the known gap 3; this answer puts his mother's rooms in Copper Row, the earlier recommendation said Ironside.
1. THE LONG WAY ROUND

FOUND: Pauline on the radio, dry as ever: "Kevin's quiet again." Or Sheila, shutting the day book on her thumb: "Ask yourself where his mileage goes, then ask Pauline. She keeps a log." Either way the place is the counter at Mickey's, on Quay Street.

OFFERED / WAITS: Offered when Sheila has opened the day book to him, or Pauline has said Kevin's name twice on the radio. Waits until Kevin's next pay day; after that Kevin stops expecting a reckoning and the matter closes as "let it lie."

STEPS:
1. The counter at Mickey's: Tom reads the day book. Kevin's fares come in short against his mileage. Sheila is there and says little.
2. The rank outside Mickey's: Kevin's car stands there between jobs. Tom can read its mileage off the dashboard; Kevin is out on a fare or at the caff, so Tom can look unseen.
3. The dispatcher's desk: Pauline has a log of Kevin's calls and gaps. Tom can ask her straight, or let her volunteer it.
4. Grace Rinaldi's caff, across the street from the rank: Kevin on his break. Tom can put it to him, or sit down and say nothing.

ENDINGS:
- Sack him. The rank is one car short. Drivers and Pauline learn the new owner reads the book.
- Keep him for a cut. A small racket starts on the rank, and the fare book lies a little more.
- Say nothing and pay the gap from his own pocket. Sheila, who keeps the cash, notices and says so [invented].
IF IT GOES WRONG: Tom asks around loudly. Kevin hears he is being looked at and quits on the rank in front of the street. The firm is short a driver, and the street talks about it.

LEDGER LINES:
- "Kevin's day fares run short of his miles. Check the car on the rank outside Mickey's, then ask Pauline at the desk."
- "Kevin takes his break at Grace's caff across the street from the rank. Catch him there before pay day."

INVENTIONS:
- Sheila notices the gap-paying from the cash she keeps. [invented]
- Pauline's log records Kevin's calls and gaps. [invented]
Fixed: The caff is across the street from Mickey's (the street's facts), not round the corner (twice).
2. TWO REAL MINUTES

FOUND: Mid-call, Pauline Kitching covers the mouthpiece and nods at the second phone on the counter. "Take this one, will you? She wants a car for the doctor's at ten, and she'll give her name to me and nobody else. Pen's by the book. Two minutes." The office is on Quay Street.
OFFERED / WAITS: Offered when Tom is behind the counter while Pauline is on another call. Waits about one minute; after that the caller rings off and the story ends in its own outcome.

STEPS:
1. Counter phone, Mickey's, Quay Street: Tom lifts the receiver. The caller, an elderly woman, wants a car at the doctor's by ten and will not give her name to him. Tom can listen, press her, or hand the phone back.
2. Same counter, Pauline still on her call: the caller gives pickup details in a rush. Tom can write them in the fare book, repeat them back, or guess a gap and move on.
3. Same counter, the call ending: Tom can promise a driver for ten, say he'll check with Pauline, or say nothing. [invented]
4. Pauline hangs up and glances at the page, then at him. Tom can own up to any gap or leave it.

ENDINGS:
- Booking right: Pauline reads the page, says "You'll do," and tells Terry Hodgson the same on the radio that night. She repeats it to Kevin Needham too. The town keeps Pauline's first word on him.
- Booking wrong: the caller is not picked up, walks, and tells the newsagent's queue Mickey's has gone to pot. Pauline hears it at the counter, says so on the radio, and both drivers hear.
- Handed back: Pauline takes the call herself, says nothing of it, and her first word on him is a shrug [invented].

IF IT GOES WRONG: The failure continues: the old woman is not collected, and the newsagent's queue talks about it for days. Tom can mend it by ringing her back through Pauline or by apologising to the queue in person. [invented]

LEDGER LINES:
- Pauline handed me the counter phone. A woman wants the doctor's by ten and will only give her name to Pauline, at the Quay Street office.
- Pauline said "You'll do." Terry and Kevin heard it on the radio, so the Hook has Pauline's first word on me.

INVENTIONS:
- The caller is an elderly woman. [invented]
- Step 3, the promise of a driver or check, is an added choice. [invented]
- The repair routes (ringing back, apologising) are added. [invented]
- The third ending, handed back. [invented]
Fixed: The added third ending (handed back) is marked [invented] and listed.
3. THE NIGHT LODGER (PASSED AS WRITTEN)

FOUND: Ian Megginson, passing the office door with his bag, stops at the front lock. "Anybody with a hairpin and an hour, that." The scratches are fresh. Ian won't say who; he says Norman Dent on the warehouse row keeps a better eye than the police.
OFFERED / WAITS: Offered once Tom has slept a night at the office and Ian has passed the door. Ian waits until the next night; after that he has stopped mentioning it.

STEPS:
1. The front lock, Mickey's door on Quay Street. Ian is there; Tom can look at the scratches, ask Ian what he'd charge to fit a new one, or ask who'd bother.
2. Norman Dent, the night watchman's hut on the warehouse row. Glad of company, he saw a light in the yard at three and swears he misses nothing. Tom can sit with him, or ask whether he'd tell anyone else.
3. The yard behind Mickey's, after midnight. Darren Milner is asleep across the back seat of the spare car. Tom can wake him, watch, or leave him and come back.
4. Tom decides, with Darren awake or asleep.

ENDINGS:
- Throw him out: Darren tells the parade that Tom is hard. The town keeps the story of a man put out with nowhere to go.
- Let him stay as a night eye on the yard: Darren becomes Tom's, and talks about it on the street. Ron notices.
- Pay Ian for a new lock and say nothing: Darren never knows he was seen; Ian knows, and so does Norman.
IF IT GOES WRONG: Tom lets the window pass. The lock is forced again, a petty loss in the yard [invented], and Norman tells the caff that the new owner did nothing about a light he'd been told of.

LEDGER LINES:
- "Ian Megginson says the front lock on Quay Street is anybody's with a hairpin and an hour. The scratches are new. Ask Norman Dent what he saw."
- "Darren Milner is asleep in the spare car in Mickey's yard. Norman Dent saw the light at three. Decide what a man with nowhere to go is worth."

INVENTIONS:
- Ian carries a bag of tools [invented].
- Norman keeps a watchman's hut on the warehouse row [invented].
- The petty loss in the yard if the window passes [invented].
- Ian quotes a price for a new lock, left to the builder [invented].
4. MICKEY'S FRIDAY

FOUND: Lily Tang, handing over Tom's first order at the takeaway on the parade, without being asked: "Same as Mickey's? Every Friday, two of number nine. I remember." Mickey is dead; the order is a debt of habit.
OFFERED / WAITS: Tom's first order at the Tangs' on a Friday. Waits on Fridays, for four weeks; after that Lily "stopped asking" and the story closes as a lapse.

STEPS:
1. Takeaway counter, the parade. Lily and Peter. Tom can say yes to the order, say no, or ask who ate the second one.
2. Quay Street rank, by the cab office door. Ron Kirby, Kevin Needham in earshot. Tom asks Ron, who goes quiet, then says "Fridays, aye."
3. Back at the counter or the rank, on a later Friday. Tom decides: take two of number nine round to Ron, let it drop, or ask Lily to stop reminding him.

ENDINGS:
- Keep Fridays with Ron: Tom brings the second portion. Ron's loyalty takes a step, and he tells Sheila. The rank sees them eating together.
- Let it lapse: Tom stops ordering two. Ron says nothing. Lily notes the gap and tells Peter.
- Ask Lily to stop: she agrees, kindly. Lily tells Peter, and Peter tells nobody, which is the point.

IF IT GOES WRONG: Four Fridays pass with no answer. Lily stops saying it, the order shrinks to one, and Ron's quiet is on the rank, where Kevin remarks on it. It continues as a thing the street noticed Tom did not pick up.

LEDGER LINES:
- Lily at the Tangs' on the parade asked for Mickey's Friday order, two of number nine. Somebody ate the second one. Ask Ron at the rank.
- Ron, at the rank, said "Fridays, aye," and no more. Decide whether Fridays are mine to keep.

INVENTIONS:
- Takeaway menu items are numbered, and "number nine" is a dish on it [invented].
- Kevin Needham is within earshot at the rank [invented].
- Lily's closing the offer by no longer mentioning it is how it lapses [invented].
Fixed: "the Parade" (the district) became "the parade", Quay Street's six bays (three times).
5. A COAT FROM THE BACK ROOM

FOUND: Tracey Scarth, pins in her mouth, at her market stall on Weighhouse Lane, or in the laundry's back room: "That's twice I've seen you in that jacket. Mickey had a good coat. Bring it me, I'll take it in two inches."
OFFERED / WAITS: Offered when Tracey has seen Tom twice in the same jacket. She waits until the market's next day.

STEPS:
1. Mickey's office, Quay Street, the hook by the radio: the coat hangs there. Pauline Kitching or Sheila Dunn may say whose it was. Tom can take it down or leave it.
2. Tracey's stall, Weighhouse Lane, Copper Row: Tracey pins it on Tom, talking as she sews. Tom can ask her to take it in, or hold it back.
3. Quay Street, the pavement outside the office: Tom walks out in it, or has it with him. June Suddaby sees it, or hears of it from someone who did.
4. Wherever June stands, or the hook if he never fetched it: Tom wears it on, offers it to her, or leaves it.

ENDINGS:
- Wear it: Tom is reshaped in Mickey's cut. The street reads him as Mickey's heir; June goes cold.
- Give it to June: she keeps it, or hands it back on her own terms.
- Leave it on the hook: the coat stays Mickey's.
The town keeps: whose coat is walking down Quay Street. Tracey tells her customers either way; the street says who wore it.

IF IT GOES WRONG: Tracey stops waiting and the coat stays on the hook, unaltered. She tells the stall: "He wouldn't be measured." Left hanging, the coat is Mickey's still, and the street notices who never touched it.

LEDGER LINES:
- Tracey, at her stall on Weighhouse Lane, will take Mickey's coat in two inches. It hangs by the radio in the office.
- June saw Mickey's coat on me outside the office on Quay Street. She said nothing, and kept walking.

INVENTIONS:
- Tracey's stall is on Weighhouse Lane, in Copper Row, since canon places Weighhouse Lane in Copper Row and the market quarter. [invented]
- The coat hangs on a hook by the radio. [invented]
- Pauline or Sheila may name the coat's owner. [invented]
- Tracey pins and alters the coat at the stall. [invented]
Fixed: The draft's second place, the laundry's back room, was restored to FOUND.
6. THE NAME ON THE BOARD (PASSED AS WRITTEN)

FOUND: Shaun Hewson, up his ladder with the pot hung on a rung, stops under Mickey's sign on Quay Street. He says: "That board by the cab rank wants doing. What's it to say?" [invented: the pot on the ladder]
OFFERED / WAITS: Offered when Shaun's boards have reached Mickey's bay. He waits 4 town hours, then paints the old name as it was.

STEPS:
1. Under the sign, Quay Street: Shaun gives Tom the brush hand-over, so to speak: he explains what he can do (the old name, or an addition) and asks what it's to say. Tom can answer him or ask the street first.
2. The cab office door: Pauline Kitching, on the radio, will say Mickey always had it done in the same cream and black [invented]. Ron Kirby, on the rank, says nothing either way but watches which Tom picks. Tom can ask either, or neither.
3. Back at the ladder: Tom rules the wording to Shaun. Shaun starts at once, whistling.
4. The pavement: while the paint goes on, Tom can stay, so his choice is seen, or walk off.

ENDINGS:
- Old name fresh painted: the street reads continuity. Shaun tells the caff the new man kept Mickey's name; Grace Rinaldi remembers it.
- Old name with "prop. T. Nowak" small underneath: the street reads a takeover, politely. Passers-by on the rank read it aloud.
- Leave it peeling: Shaun tells the caff the new man doesn't care.
IF IT GOES WRONG: Past 4 hours Shaun paints the old name as it was and moves to the next bay; the sign is Mickey's, fresh, and Tom never said a word. Shaun shrugs it off at the caff.

LEDGER LINES:
- Shaun, the sign painter, waits under Mickey's board on Quay Street, brush in hand. He wants to know what the sign says.
- Mickey's board has been painted over. The street has already read it, and Shaun has told the caff.

INVENTIONS:
- The pot hung on the ladder rung. [invented]
- Pauline's remark that Mickey used cream and black. [invented]
- Ron watching which wording Tom picks. [invented]
- Grace Rinaldi, at the caff, hearing Shaun's report. [invented]
7. A RIDE FOR THE SERGEANT

FOUND: Rain after dark; the office phone goes and Pauline holds it out, dry: "It's the police. She wants a car." Her words: "Carol Ellis, her motor's died on her by the fish market, at the shed end. She'll stand there till she's wet through."
OFFERED / WAITS: Raining, after dark, Ellis has met Tom once. She waits 30 town minutes, then walks.

STEPS:
1. Mickey's, the radio desk on Quay Street. Pauline and Terry Hodgson, in from the rank. Terry takes the job without being asked; Tom can ride along, send Terry alone, or refuse the fare.
2. The fish market, Ellis beside her dead car, under the shed roof. If Tom came, he can talk or stay quiet; she starts the conversation either way. If Terry came, she questions him.
3. The back of the cab, rain on the glass. Tom can answer plainly, deflect, or say nothing; she learns what he says and how he says it.
4. The drop, where she names, outside Mickey's or short of it. She pays the fare, and what she says at the door is the last thing Tom hears.

ENDINGS:
- Ride with her: a live talk. Ellis keeps how he spoke, evasive or plain, and weighs the next meeting by it.
- Terry alone: Terry tells Tom what she asked, or says "nothing" and means it. Terry's version goes to Kevin Needham.
- Refused: Ellis walks home in the rain and remembers. The rank hears she was left standing.
IF IT GOES WRONG: Past 30 minutes she walks, soaked, and the story ends as "refused" in its own outcome. Ron and Kevin talk about it by morning, and nothing is lost but her good opinion.

LEDGER LINES:
- Ellis's car is dead by the fish market, at the shed end. Terry has taken the cab; I could ride along.
- Terry says the sergeant asked him nothing. He drove her home from the shed end.

INVENTIONS:
- Pauline's line naming the fish market's shed end as the car's spot. [invented]
- Terry offering the job unprompted. [invented]
- The drop point being Ellis's choice and the fare paid in cash. [invented]
- The rank hearing she was left standing. [invented]
Fixed: Tannery Row (Ironside) was cut from the fish market's place (three times).
8. HADDOCK'S DEAR (PASSED AS WRITTEN)

FOUND: Brenda, loud at her counter in the fish shop on Quay Street, to anyone listening: "Short again, four boxes of haddock, and somebody's signing my name for them. Down the fish market railing, first light. Go and look." [invented: the shop stands on Quay Street]
OFFERED / WAITS: Offered once Tom has spoken to Brenda once. She waits 3 dawns, then stops waiting and settles it her own way.

STEPS:
1. The fish market railing at first light. Brenda is buying; Tom can watch, ask her where the count falls short, or ask a passing porter.
2. The loading bay beside the railing. The porter who signs for her boxes, a stranger to the cast [invented], is signing under her name. Tom can watch, count, or put it to him.
3. The weighing hut by the quay gate. The syndicate's man takes the porters' cut here. He names nothing and sees who asks, unless Tom has a way in. [invented: the hut]
4. Back at the counter, Tom reports to Brenda, or settles it unreported.

ENDINGS:
- Catch the porter: a word or fists, seen on the dock. The porters see how Tom handles it, Brenda is repaid, and the porter's cut goes unpaid and unmentioned.
- Pay Brenda's loss, say nothing: no one on the dock learns it happened. Brenda keeps the money and the grudge-free air; the porter carries on.
- Ask the Widow's people: it is sorted at once, and the dock knows whose favour Tom asked.
IF IT GOES WRONG: The porter sees him coming and the dock closes ranks. Tom gets no answer at the railing, and Brenda tells everyone he tried.
The town keeps: Brenda's version, which the whole parade hears by noon.

LEDGER LINES:
- Brenda's haddock is coming up short. Find who signs for her boxes at the fish market railing, first light.
- Porter at the loading bay is signing Brenda's name. The syndicate's man at the weighing hut takes his cut.

INVENTIONS:
- The fish shop stands on Quay Street. [invented]
- The loading bay and the weighing hut by the quay gate are places on the fish dock. [invented]
- The porter is a stranger to the cast, unnamed. [invented]
- The syndicate's man is unnamed and sits at the hut. [invented]
9. TWELVE WEEKS' NOTICE

FOUND: Tom passes the kiosk on Quay Street. Julie Kettlewell tells whoever is near: "Twelve years on them presses and twelve weeks' notice. Generous, they called it. And the last weeks' money never came. Go and ask at the steam laundry, the one with the tall chimney." [invented]
OFFERED / WAITS: Offered when Tom passes the kiosk while Julie is there. She waits 6 town hours, then takes a job across town and the story ends.

STEPS:
1. The laundry's office, its side door off the yard: a clerk behind a hatch says the owner is in and nothing is owed. Tom can ask for the pay book or ask for the owner.
2. The owner's room above the presses: Tom can press politely, lean on him, or leave. Either way the owner will not name a date.
3. The presses' early shift: Doreen Harland saw the packets made up and says the sums were short. Tom can ask her to say so to the owner, or keep what she told him.
4. Back to Julie at the kiosk, or to the office on Quay Street to settle it there.

ENDINGS:
- Lean on the owner: he pays Julie in full and tells Christine Pickering at the harbour office he was threatened. The town keeps that Mickey's still frightens people, and a clerk has heard it.
- Pay her from the office: Sheila marks it in the book. The town keeps that the office pays its own, and Sheila knows the figure.
- Job on the phone beside Pauline Kitching: Julie takes it. The town keeps that Mickey's takes on the laid off, and who counts as its own has changed.

IF IT GOES WRONG: If Tom lets the six hours pass, Julie takes work across town and says on the street that Mickey's never came. Doreen is left carrying what she told him, and the owner knows someone asked.

LEDGER LINES:
- Julie Kettlewell, at the kiosk on Quay Street, is owed her last weeks' money by the steam laundry. Ask at the laundry's office.
- Doreen Harland, early shift at the presses, saw the pay packets made up. She will say they were short.

INVENTIONS:
- The laundry has a tall chimney [invented].
- The owner has an upstairs room above the presses [invented].
- The pay book is kept at the clerk's hatch [invented].
- Christine Pickering is the harbour office clerk who hears the owner's complaint [invented].
Fixed: The kiosk and the steam laundry are on Quay Street (the street's places): Weighhouse Lane and the tannery wall were cut.
10. THE LAUNDRY'S HAMPERS

FOUND: Doreen Harland stands at the steam laundry's side door with a stack of hampers and no van. "Your lot could carry these for us. Mickey would have. The door by the loading step." [invented: the loading step]
OFFERED / WAITS: Offered when Mickey's has a spare car on the rank in daytime. Doreen waits until the van is mended (2 days), then stops waiting.

STEPS:
1. Side door, steam laundry: Doreen and her hampers, a stack of eight [invented]. Tom can ask what she wants carried, how often and what she can pay, or walk on.
2. The rank, Quay Street: Kevin Needham sits with the spare car. Tom can ask Kevin to run a load, or ask Ron what Mickey did. Kevin moans about the smell in his car.
3. Back at the laundry: Doreen names a price for the daily run, twice a day. Tom can accept it, push for more, or refuse.
4. Mickey's office: Tom tells Pauline Kitching the run is on, so she can put it on the radio, and Sheila Dunn sees the figure. She asks why it is so low if it is.

ENDINGS:
- Take the contract: clean money enters the fare book, Kevin and Terry Hodgson grumble about the hampers. The town keeps the cab office's name on the laundry's run, seen twice a day.
- Turn it down: Doreen finds another way. The town keeps that Mickey's no longer does what Mickey did.
- Take it at a price too low to be clean: Sheila asks about it, and the town still sees the cars on the run.

IF IT GOES WRONG: Doreen stops waiting once the van is mended. She says so at the side door, not unkindly, and the laundry's run goes on without Mickey's. The street notes who offered and who said no, and Doreen tells anyone who asks.

LEDGER LINES:
- "Doreen Harland wants the laundry's hampers carried. Side door, by the loading step. Her van's out for two days."
- "Doreen's price is in. Sheila will ask what the run is worth. The cab with the hampers is seen at the laundry twice daily."

INVENTIONS:
- The laundry's side door is by a loading step. [invented]
- The stack is eight hampers. [invented]
Fixed: The steam laundry is on Quay Street, not Tannery Row (three times).
11. THE WINDOW AT THE CAFF
FOUND: Tom walks past the caff and finds the front window boarded, Grace on the step with a broom. "Don't ask who. No police, and no fists either. Come in when you've had a think,"
OFFERED / WAITS: Offered once Grace knows Tom by name. She waits until the glazier comes, 2 days; after that she has "dealt with it herself."

STEPS:
1. The caff, Quay Street: Grace behind the counter, boards on the glass. Tom can ask, offer help, or leave; she repeats her two rules.
2. Tracey's market stall, Copper Row, sewing as she talks: she saw "a young lad running, new jacket, fair hair," heading for the quay end. Tom can ask her to keep it quiet.
3. The corner by the pawn on Quay Street: the newest of Danny Cammack's crew, about twenty, loitering and nervous. Tom can talk him round, threaten, or walk away.
4. Back at the caff, or the yard behind it: Tom brings him, hands him on, or leaves him.

ENDINGS:
- Pots: the lad washes Grace's pots for a week. Grace tells the counter Tom did it her way; the street hears it, and the crew hears he sent one back whole.
- Ellis: Tom hands him to DS Carol Ellis. Grace says at the counter, loudly, that it is police after all; Ellis owes him a small favour, and the crew hear who gave a lad up.

LEDGER LINES:
- "Grace's window is boarded and she wants no police and no fists. Tracey, at her stall on Copper Row, saw a lad running."
- "The young one from Cammack's crew is on the corner by Rita's pawn. Grace is waiting at the caff."

INVENTIONS:
- Tracey saw fair hair and a new jacket. [invented]
- The lad loiters by Rita's pawn on Quay Street. [invented]
- Ellis owes Tom a small favour after the handover. [invented]
- Grace's tea comes slower on the failure branch. [invented]
Fixed: The Tivoli was cut from Grace's line: canon gives the Tivoli no place on Quay Street (known gap 4).
12. CLOSING TIME AT THE TANGS' (PASSED AS WRITTEN)

FOUND: Lily, wiping down the counter and not looking up, on his third visit: "It's the same lot every night about closing. Stand on the parade by the takeaway's window and you'll hear it, but not from us." No words reach him from inside, only the noise. Peter says it is nothing.
OFFERED / WAITS: Offered once Lily has served Tom twice. Waits three closing times, then it goes on without him and the giver "stopped waiting".

STEPS:
1. The Tangs' takeaway on the parade, an hour before closing: Lily and Peter at the counter. Tom can eat, ask Lily plainly, or let Peter's "it's nothing" stand.
2. The same counter at closing, night one. Four or five men in their twenties at the window, the leader at the front; Lily's face. Tom can stand at the counter, stand aside, or leave.
3. Quay Street, the cab office, any evening: Ron, who can be asked to come, and Pauline or a driver who has heard it. Tom can ask Ron to stand at the counter.
4. The corner by the shuttered newsagent's, after the men leave: Tom can speak to the men, quietly or in front of the parade.
5. Closing, last night: whichever of the above Tom has chosen, or none.

ENDINGS:
- Presence alone: Tom stands at the counter and the men lose interest. Lily remembers who stood there, and tells her regulars. The town keeps: who stood at the counter.
- Humiliation: Tom shames the leader in front of the parade. It ends, and Danny Cammack's crew notice who did it. The town keeps: the leader's face, and that Tom did it.
- Nothing: it goes on. The regulars see Tom not see it, and say so.
IF IT GOES WRONG: After the third closing it continues without him; Lily stops mentioning it, and the regulars on the parade know he was told and did not come.

LEDGER LINES:
- "Lily at the takeaway on the parade says a crowd shouts at her window at closing. Peter says nothing's wrong. Stand there tonight, or send Ron."
- "The men at the takeaway's window were seen off, or weren't. Lily knows who stood at her counter. Whoever it was, the parade noticed."

INVENTIONS:
- Lily says she cannot hear what is shouted from inside, so Tom hears only noise. [invented]
- The corner by the shuttered newsagent's as the place to speak to the men. [invented]
- The number of men, four or five, with one leader. [invented]
13. OFF THE BACK OF A LORRY (PASSED AS WRITTEN)
FOUND: Darren is on the Quay Street pavement outside the office with a crate. "Ten each to you, and I owe you anyway. Come and look, they're by the wall."
OFFERED / WAITS: Offered when Darren owes the office and Tom has cash on him. Darren waits 2 town hours, then packs the crate and sells them elsewhere.

STEPS:
1. Outside the office, Quay Street pavement: Darren and the crate, a lamp-post at his back. Tom can look, ask where they're from (Darren laughs it off), haggle, or walk on.
2. The same spot: Tom picks buy, refuse, or pay-off. Pay-off means Darren's debt cleared in radios, set against the book: Tom names a number, Darren counts them out.
3. Inside the office: Pauline or Kevin sees the radio come in. Tom can tune it, stand it on the counter, or hide it.
4. Later, on the pavement or at the rank: the chandler's man walks past and looks. Tom can own up, deny it, or point at Darren. [invented]

ENDINGS:
